embedded_ivos.text:
Anthropic’s AI safety proposal falls far short of protecting public health and safety. Congress must go further.

We’re facing huge risk from even the current generation of frontier AI models, and that risk will only escalate with further model development. Government’s most basic obligation is to protect public health and safety. In the context of AI, that means Congress must ensure that AI benefits people and doesn’t harm people. Quick, effective, robust regulation is essential.

Several provisions in Anthropic’s proposal go beyond what has been proposed in Congress so far, but big picture, this proposal is insufficient to manage the catastrophic AI risks about which Anthropic, other companies, and many experts are warning us.

Anthropic’s proposal contains no minimum standards for AI companies’ safety plans or for third party auditors, and the proposal would make it even harder for the federal government or states to nimbly regulate and act to prevent severe harms. If we’re going to have safety standards and auditors — and we must — it’s essential that regulators have flexible authority to ensure they are actually protecting people.

The proposal also uses a definition from SB 53 that was intended for risk disclosures — not for broader regulation — and extends that definition to dramatically limit the situations in which the federal government can stop model deployments. SB 53 was the first AI safety regulation in the country. It is a transparency law, and we intended it to be the first step, not the final step, to protect people from catastrophic risk. Misuse of that law’s definition would effectively gut the emergency shutdown provisions in this proposal.

The state law preemption in Anthropic’s proposal also goes too far. Given the abuse we’ve seen by the Trump administration — toward Anthropic earlier this year and more recently when Trump and Musk colluded to disable Starlink/Starshield for Ukraine, as part of their corrupt love affair with Putin — it’s perfectly reasonable to be concerned about corrupt government actors using shutdown powers to attack disfavored companies. Yet, given the scale of the risks about which these companies and many others are warning us, as well as the turbulence of our federal politics, tying the hands of regulators in California and other states is not a good idea.

There are several stronger policy proposals, around auditing, creation of a regulator, and various other issues, that are under development now. Policymakers should look to these proposals as the basis for action in the coming weeks and months.

We have very little time to get this right, and we must act with urgency. We must ensure Congressional action protects public health and safety and doesn’t undermine it.

deepseek.reason: The speaker supports third-party auditors and auditing generally, but does not mention embedded or on-site independent access.
deepseek.confidence_reason: The statement addresses general auditors, not the narrower embedded IVO proposal.

embedded_ivos.text:
The smartest AI minds on the planet are my constituents, and they’ve been warning for years that the risk of runaway AI causing a catastrophe is very real. 

It was because of those warnings that I introduced the nation’s first AI safety bill in 2023, alongside an incredible coalition of youth activists, cutting edge researchers, labor unions, and safety advocates. We were called every name in the book — decels, Luddites, alarmists — and were told not to worry because these were ‘science fiction risks.’ That bill, SB 1047, would have required large AI models to have emergency shutdown ability aka kill switches and would have subjected AI labs to liability for releasing dangerous models that caused catastrophic harm.

These risks aren’t science fiction — they’re here and now. And we have to act as soon as possible if we’re going to prevent them from harming people. 

Last week I joined with other leading AI-focused state legislators to call on the AI labs to slow the pace of development until research on AI safety, alignment, and transparency can catch up. These systems are advancing alarmingly quickly, and the labs have a moral responsibility to change course before real people suffer the consequences.

We also urgently need government action to build on the work we started here in California. Congress must pass real safety standards backed by strong enforcement, and create a new regulatory body to respond nimbly to a rapidly changing field. We need third party verification and steep fines for noncompliance with safety standards. We need to protect jobs and workers and invest in up-skilling and reskilling people for the new age we’re entering.

We’ve been warned. With social media and data privacy, we’ve seen what happens when government ignores obvious red flags from a powerful new technology. 

What matters now is that we act with urgency. Let’s get it done.

deepseek.reason: The statement calls for third-party verification but not embedded, on-site, or ongoing internal independent auditors.
deepseek.confidence_reason: Third-party verification alone is explicitly insufficient for the embedded-IVO target.

My statement with @Sen_Gounardes, @AlexBores @MaryforIL @DanielDidech_IL on urgent need for legislative and industry action on AI safety:

Lawmakers Behind State AI Safety Laws Call For Industry-Wide AI Safety Pact to Protect the Public

“As the AI labs race to create ever more powerful AI systems, the question of how we can best protect the public from the risks they present has become even more urgent. This question was thrown into sharp relief by recent reports of AI agents scheming on how to cheat tests, hacking companies in the real world, and even trying to trick humans into installing malicious software. 

“These behaviors are alarming and should serve as a warning shot to us all. If researchers cannot reliably prevent their models from going rogue, much of our digital infrastructure and the essential systems that keep our society running are at risk.

“As the lead lawmakers behind the three strongest state-level frontier AI safety laws enacted in the country (so far), we believe that the frontier labs must engage with the seriousness of purpose that this moment demands. Given the urgency, we call on them to work together to eliminate the risk that a catastrophe will result from their rush to build highly capable AI systems before solving problems of alignment and safety.

“Coordinated initiatives to pace the frontier of AI development are likely the only mechanisms capable of preventing such a catastrophe. It is critical that frontier labs work together until progress on alignment and safety have demonstrably surpassed the breakneck pace of their race to produce highly capable AI systems.

“We call on all frontier AI laboratories to immediately establish a Mutually Agreed Pacing Framework (MAP Framework) that is jointly negotiated and independently verifiable by third parties.

“To be clear, we do not view this as a replacement for robust actions at the state, federal, and/or international levels. We are simply responding to the speed of developments by asking everyone to play their part, recognizing that the pace of these advancements is likely to exceed the current speed of government action. The frontier labs have the technical expertise and the moral responsibility to take extraordinary action to address the challenges they have set in motion. We urge them to establish this framework immediately.”

deepseek.reason: The statement calls for third-party verification of a pacing framework but not embedded, on-site, or ongoing internal independent auditors.
deepseek.confidence_reason: It endorses independent third-party verification, which the rubric says is insufficient for embedded IVOs.
